paras: The Franklin County moonshiners' attacks on Black residents were a series of whippings, robberies and expulsions carried out in late April 1881 by a disguised band led by the illicit distiller Dave Gillespie in the Running Bog neighborhood of Franklin County, Virginia. The band accused its victims of informing to federal revenue officers and ordered thirteen of them to leave the county on pain of death. Known only through the report of the revenue agent who had raided the district, the episode was carried nationally as a 'revival of Ku-Kluxism' and as evidence of local officials' indifference.

In March 1881 a federal raid on illicit distilleries in southwestern Virginia destroyed a large still on Runnel Bog creek in Franklin County run by Dave Gillespie. The same dispatch said the district was 'infested with armed squads of illicit distillers' waiting for the revenue officers. Internal Revenue Agent Tracie later led another raid in Running Bog 'on the 20th', which one wire copy dated April 20, in an attempt to capture Gillespie; it failed when Gillespie escaped from his house.

According to Tracie's report, Gillespie 'and his crowd of supporters' then turned on Black residents of the neighborhood, whom they charged with having given information to the revenue officers. The men went in disguise with their faces blackened, whipped men and women, robbed one or two of money, destroyed property, and drove people from their homes, some of them half naked. They formed thirteen of the victims into one party on the road to West Virginia and ordered them to leave, warning that they would be killed if they returned.

None of the victims was named, and no deaths were reported. A news-summary item in the Connecticut Western News added that in some cases houses were burned, a detail absent from the agent's quoted report.

Tracie offered a $100 reward to anyone who would lodge Gillespie in jail, but wrote that 'few seem anxious to undertake the capture of this notorious desperado.' He reported that the outrages had not disturbed Franklin County officials 'in the slightest degree' and that citizens were too frightened even to speak of them. He also faulted the United States Marshal's office, and the Richmond Dispatch said he expected soon to make another attempt to capture Gillespie. No report of Gillespie's arrest, or of any prosecution for the attacks, appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press as a Washington dispatch dated May 3, 1881, summarizing the report Tracie had forwarded to Commissioner of Internal Revenue Raum. On May 4 it ran in the New-York Tribune, the Wheeling Intelligencer and Register, the Richmond Dispatch, the National Republican, the Chicago Tribune and two California dailies, and over the following week in papers from Memphis, Knoxville, Bismarck and Dallas to Somerset, Pennsylvania.

Headlines put the moonshiners rather than the victims at the center: 'Virginia Moonshiners', 'Moonshiner Miscreants', 'The Desperado Gillispie' and 'Captain Tracie After the King of the 'Shiners.' Others stressed the breakdown of law, as in the New-York Tribune's 'Lawlessness in Virginia' with the deck 'Officers of Justice Indifferent', or the Klan parallel, as in the Wheeling Intelligencer's 'A Kuklux Revival' and the Chicago Tribune's 'An Army Needed in Virginia.' Within the dispatch itself the agent's words, 'shameful outrages upon innocent colored people', set the tone, and short news-summary items repeated that many Black people had been 'Ku-Kluxed' in the county.

Transmission varied the details: some western copies spelled the agent 'Tracy' or 'Grace', raised the reward to $1,000, or reduced the whipping victims to 'a man and woman', and two Southern copies said the outrages had terrorized 'colored citizens' rather than 'good citizens.' No account from the victims themselves or from a Franklin County paper appears in the coverage.
Whether houses were burned rests on a single unattributed news item, while the agent's own report speaks only of destroyed property.

accounts.label: Revenue agent's report (Washington wire)
accounts.gist: Since his raid on the 20th, Gillespie and his disguised supporters had whipped, robbed and driven out Black residents they accused of informing, ordering thirteen to leave for West Virginia on penalty of death, while county officials were unmoved.

accounts.label: News-summary briefs
accounts.gist: Short items said many Black people had been 'Ku-Kluxed' in Franklin County, whipped, robbed and driven out; one added that some houses were burned.

framing.detail: The agent's own words, carried in every copy, called the acts 'shameful outrages upon innocent colored people' and a 'revival of Ku-Kluxism'; the New-York Tribune added the deck 'Negroes Whipped, Robbed and Driven from Their Homes—Officers of Justice Indifferent'.
Most papers ran the Washington dispatch with headlines centered on the moonshiners and Gillespie ('Virginia Moonshiners', 'Moonshiner Miscreants', 'The Desperado Gillispie') rather than the victims.

conflicts.note: Variant wording in the western wire copies; the eastern and Virginia texts agree on 'men and women'.
The larger figure appears only in two California papers' copies, likely a transmission error.
The burning appears only in an unattributed news-summary item and not in the agent's quoted report.
